title: One sentence runs the whole system
paras: Here's the one sentence that runs the whole system. Every planning decision in England must be made in accordance with the development plan, unless material considerations indicate otherwise. That fixes your method: you don't start with national policy, or the objections, or the outcome you'd like — you read the plan as a whole, form a view on whether the proposal accords, and only then ask whether material considerations point the other way. Reverse those steps and the decision's vulnerable. The citations, I'll leave to the written guide.

A second provision reinforces it: have regard to the development plan, to local finance considerations, and to any other material considerations. So, two stages. Stage one, the plan position — read the plan whole, identify the relevant policies, reach a view, accords or conflicts overall. A scheme can breach one policy and satisfy others; the question is the balance across the whole plan, not a single clause.

Stage two, the tug of war — now national policy and the other material considerations answer one thing: do they indicate a decision otherwise than in accordance with the plan? And the development plan is the adopted local plan or plans; any neighbourhood plan that's passed referendum, which then forms part of the statutory plan at full weight, not that of a mere material consideration; minerals and waste plans; and where relevant the spatial development strategy — in London, the London Plan. Where two documents conflict, the later-adopted policy wins.

The plan-led system isn't a presumption the plan is right — it's a discipline that the plan is the starting point, outweighed only after it's correctly identified. The test: an officer who can't say in one sentence whether the proposal accords with the plan as a whole hasn't yet started the decision.

title: Materiality is law; weight is judgement
paras: Next — materiality is law, but weight is judgement, and confusing the two separates a planner who decides from one who only quotes policy. Whether a consideration is material is a question of law: it's material if it relates to the use and development of land and serves a planning purpose — that's Stringer. How much weight it carries is judgement, and provided it's material and the decision's rational, that weight is for the decision-maker, not the courts. Which is why two competent planners can weigh the same facts differently and both be acting lawfully.

So the court polices the boundary — is this capable of being material at all — but it doesn't re-weigh. And there's a third distinction: interpreting a policy is law, applying it is judgement. The meaning of a plan policy is an objective question of law, read in context; how it lands on the facts, and the weight the compliance or conflict attracts, is judgement. On a statutory challenge that's decisive — interpretation you can fight as law, weight only on rationality.

The reading worth carrying into practice is purposive. Policies are instruments for outcomes, not ends in themselves — so ask what a policy is for, what harm it guards against. A proposal might breach the letter while leaving the purpose unharmed, and that weakens the weight of the conflict; or comply with the letter in a way that defeats the purpose, which weakens the value of the compliance. That's where a technical breach can be argued down to a neutral, or even a positive, finding.

title: When the plan, the Framework and a minister disagree
paras: Now — what happens when the plan, national policy and a minister all seem to say different things? It's resolved by legal status first, then rational weight, then reasons. Nothing lower in the ladder overrides something higher as a matter of law, so the argument is almost always about weight, not authority. The precise citations are in the written guide.

The ladder: statute sits above everything — and in particular the statutory duties that are mandatory obligations, not mere considerations. The heritage duties and the habitats regime impose hard tests you can't just weigh away. Beneath statute sits the development plan — the statutory starting point — which policy and guidance don't override as a matter of law.

National policy — the National Planning Policy Framework — is government policy, a material consideration of great weight. But it isn't statute and isn't part of the development plan, so it doesn't change the plan's primacy. Hopkins Homes settled that: the presumption works through the weight you give plan policies, not by displacing the statute. So 'national policy says something different' is usually really the question — how out of date is the relevant plan policy? Below the Framework sits Planning Practice Guidance: it explains how to apply the Framework, carries less weight, and can't contradict it.

Ministerial statements sit on a gradient. A formal written ministerial statement is a material consideration and can carry real weight — onshore wind, Article 4 directions and housing delivery have all been steered by these ahead of the Framework. But it doesn't amend the plan or override statute. Below it, a recovered-appeal or call-in decision shows the direction of ministerial thinking but weighs less; a speech or press release barely registers. And emerging and neighbourhood plans take weight from the stage reached, the unresolved objections, and their consistency with the Framework.

Two more sources. Previous appeal decisions matter, because consistency is itself a consideration — depart from a relevant earlier decision on similar facts and you must explain why, though each turns on its facts and none is binding precedent. And supplementary planning documents, design codes and local guidance are material, with weight by status and currency. So: legal status, rational weight, clear reasons.

title: The tilted balance, and how to spot it
paras: The tilted balance, and how to spot it — the most consequential switch in English decision-making. In decision-taking, where there's no relevant plan policy, or the policies most important for the application are out of date, the exercise reframes: grant permission unless the adverse impacts significantly and demonstrably outweigh the benefits, against national policy as a whole. That's markedly more applicant-friendly than 'does this accord with the plan', and spotting the trigger is often worth more than any substantive argument.

The presumption in favour of sustainable development has two limbs, plan-making and decision-taking. The decision-taking limb engages in those two situations — no relevant policies, or the most important ones out of date. In housing, they're out of date where the authority can't demonstrate the required supply of deliverable sites. But the supply period, the buffers and the wording change between editions, so check the current version rather than reciting it.

Two carve-outs before you conclude the balance is tilted your way. First, it doesn't apply where specific policies protecting particular assets give a clear reason for refusal — typically habitats sites, sites of special scientific interest, designated heritage assets, land at risk of flooding, and protected landscapes. Second, even when engaged, it's a balance, not a grant: the adverse impacts can still win if they significantly and demonstrably outweigh the benefits.

So the tilt swaps plan-conflict for a benefits-against-harms test weighted to approval. The sequence: establish the plan position anyway, since it still frames weight; test whether the presumption's engaged, including supply; check the protective policies; and if it applies and none bite, run the significantly-and-demonstrably test against national policy as a whole. This loops back to Hopkins Homes — the tilt is how out-of-date policies lose weight, not a freestanding override of the statute. It's the plan-led duty operating through weight.

title: Duties, not considerations
paras: Duties, not considerations. Some things get weighed; some constrain. Statutory duties — heritage and habitats above all — don't go on the scales as ordinary considerations. They work as thresholds, or strong presumptions the proposal must clear before you reach the ordinary balance. Miss that and you can build a tidy benefits-against-harms table that's unlawful, because it's weighed away a duty that was never yours to weigh.

Heritage: the listed building and conservation area duties require special regard to preserving a listed building and its setting, and special attention to preserving or enhancing a conservation area's character and appearance. The courts give these considerable importance and weight — harm to a designated asset isn't one factor in a level balance; it carries a strong presumption against grant that must be clearly outweighed. The detail's in the heritage guide; the point is that it's a duty, not a consideration.

Habitats: the regime imposes hard tests around European sites. Where a plan or project is likely to have a significant effect, you carry out an appropriate assessment, and you can only agree once you've ascertained it won't adversely affect the site's integrity — save the strict imperative-reasons derogation. That's a threshold: fail it and it cannot be permitted, however great the benefits.

Nutrient neutrality and recreational impacts on European sites are still fast-moving, so check the file. But the lesson holds: run the duty or hard test first, as a gateway, then reach the ordinary balance for what's genuinely to be weighed. A table that's absorbed a heritage duty, or an appropriate-assessment failure, isn't a balance — it's an error of law dressed as one.

title: The reasons are the decision
paras: The reasons are the decision. Writing the reasons is the discipline of making it — if you can't articulate why the benefits outweigh the harms, you haven't finished weighing them. Reasons must be intelligible and adequate, and they must grapple with the principal important controversial issues. A defensible outcome with hollow reasons is a decision waiting to be quashed.

The standard: reasons must let the reader understand why it was decided as it was, and what was concluded on the principal controversial issues, without leaving a substantial doubt that the decision-maker erred. They can be briefly stated — the particularity depends on the issues.

For local authorities the duty isn't confined to refusals. The routine requirement to give full reasons for every grant was pared back, but a common-law duty can still arise — notably where members grant against officer advice, on a matter of significant public interest, or where the reasoning otherwise isn't apparent. So in committee, assume any departure from the officer recommendation must be minuted with intelligible planning reasons, at the time.

The craft point: write the balance as a sequence of reasoned weightings, not a conclusion. Each main consideration, the weight given, and why; address the contrary points; then the overall conclusion. Built that way, an officer report or committee minute is both a better decision and a far harder target on challenge — because it shows the controversial issues were confronted, not glossed.

title: Things that feel material and aren’t
paras: Now — things that feel material, and aren't. There's a short list that's reliably non-material: a private view, property values, boundary and covenant disputes, competition, the applicant's identity. But several are non-material only until a genuine planning consequence is shown. The skill is spotting the moment a red herring picks up a land-use consequence and becomes material after all.

The reliable ones: loss of a private view — no right to a view; property values; boundary, covenant and other private legal disputes; loss of trade to a competitor — competition isn't a planning consideration, though the consequences of vacancy or lost vitality may be; the applicant's identity or motives; and matters for other regimes — building regulations, licensing, environmental permitting — bar a genuine land-use overlap.

Then the ones non-material until a consequence appears. Construction disturbance — temporary, usually controllable by condition, but weighty where prolonged or acute. Fear and perceived risk — exceptionally material where the perception has a real effect on the use and enjoyment of land, even if the fear is objectively unfounded. And need for the development — not generally required, but it can add positive weight, and it's central to some tests, like rural-worker dwellings.

And three genuinely material but routinely mishandled. The fallback — a realistic alternative the applicant could carry out without the permission sought, whether extant permitted-development rights or an extant permission; weight depends on how real the prospect is, and a real prospect of a comparable but less desirable outcome can be decisive, especially on householder and change-of-use cases. Precedent — capable of being material, but it must be evidenced, not asserted: you have to show a real difficulty resisting like cases, and a bare floodgates argument gets rejected. Prematurity — narrowly confined, rarely justified except where the proposal's so substantial and the emerging plan so advanced that granting would predetermine central decisions; it seldom succeeds, so argue it sparingly. And one committee discipline: the volume of objection isn't itself material — the merits are, the number isn't.

title: The considerations scale with the proposal
paras: One framing point before the worked examples. The doctrine so far is one framework, but it doesn't apply identically to every application. As a proposal grows, the material considerations grow, and the decisive question climbs — from amenity, to principle, to the overall balance and housing supply. And statutory duties, or the tilt, can displace the plan-led starting point. What follows works it through eight types, from a householder extension to a major greenfield scheme.

Two things throughout. The typical weights I suggest are practice and judgement, not law — calibrate them to the plan and the evidence. And the skill isn't listing every consideration present; it's spotting which are decisive. An extension turns on amenity and character; a countryside dwelling on the principle; a major scheme on the overall balance and whether the tilt's engaged. Read to the type nearest your case — but answer the decisive question first.

title: Applying it: the householder extension
paras: The worked examples, then — starting with the householder extension. At an existing dwelling the principle isn't in issue; it's won or lost on the character of the dwelling and street scene, and the amenity of the neighbours. Almost everything else is secondary.

On character: scale, proportion, materials, and whether the extension is subservient to the host — usually the decisive strand. On amenity: overlooking and loss of privacy; loss of light and overshadowing — the forty-five and twenty-five degree rules of thumb, and the B-R-E daylight and sunlight guidance where genuinely in issue; and any overbearing or enclosing effect. Highways and parking rarely decide these; trees count only where amenity trees or a preservation order are affected; and there's no statutory duty unless the dwelling's listed or in a conservation area, when the heritage duties engage.

The point people forget is the permitted-development fallback: a real prospect of building something comparable without consent is material, and frequently decisive. Against it, dismiss the red herrings — a private view, property value, boundary or covenant disputes, a neighbour's own extension as precedent. The decisive question is whether the extension stays subservient and protects the neighbours' living conditions. Conditions cover the time limit, matching materials, and obscure or non-opening windows; obligations, normally none.

title: Applying it: a new house in a settlement
paras: A single new house in a settlement — infill or a garden plot — adds a principle-and-location layer on top of the amenity questions. First: is the principle of a new dwelling acceptable here — inside the settlement boundary, a sustainable spot, and does the plan support or resist infill?

Once the principle's arguable, the design must sit in context — grain, density, plot pattern, sympathetic infill rather than garden-grabbing and town-cramming. Amenity runs both ways: to the neighbours, and for the future occupiers, whose living conditions — amenity space, light, outlook — are themselves material. Then access and highway safety; foul and surface-water drainage, with the flood-risk sequential test in a flood zone; trees and any preservation order; and ecology, including mandatory biodiversity net gain. Heritage duties if the site's designated or affects a designated setting; habitats only near a European site.

The decisive question is whether the principle's acceptable here and the design sits comfortably in context. Precedent is usually overstated; loss of view, property value and personal need aren't material. Conditions cover approved plans, materials, landscaping, drainage and sustainable drainage, ecology and net gain, and obscure glazing. Obligations may secure off-site net gain, and the community infrastructure levy applies where the authority charges — though affordable housing's usually below threshold on a plot this small.

title: Applying it: a new house in the countryside
paras: A new house in open countryside is decided on the principle — almost nothing else matters until it's cleared. New isolated homes are resisted, save a narrow set of exceptions, and a scheme outside them won't be rescued by good design or amenity.

The exceptions: an essential need for a rural worker to live at the site; re-use or redevelopment of a redundant or disused building; an optimal-viability heritage case; a dwelling of truly outstanding design; and sub-division of an existing dwelling. And whether a site is even 'isolated' is a question of fact and judgement — it means physically, not functionally, isolated, so a dwelling near a hamlet may not be isolated at all, which changes the policy that applies. Only once the principle's arguable do the usual strands follow — landscape and character, heritage setting, highways, amenity, drainage and ecology.

Statutory duties often bite out here — heritage setting; the great weight owed to a protected landscape, a National Landscape or Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty; and habitats near a European site. A wish to live rurally, family or personal circumstances, an abstract 'need' — little or no weight. The decisive question is whether the proposal falls within a recognised exception. Where it does, the usual conditions are an occupancy condition for a rural-worker case, removal of permitted-development rights, and landscaping and materials — occasionally an obligation tying it to the holding.

title: Applying it: the rural worker’s dwelling
paras: The rural worker's dwelling turns on an essential need for a worker to live permanently at or near the workplace — and a financially sound enterprise behind that need. Functional need is the gateway: does the enterprise genuinely require a worker readily available on site, for animal welfare or security?

Beyond that, the enterprise must be established and capable of sustaining a dwelling — a new one is usually tested with a temporary permission first. And could the need be met by accommodation already on or near the holding? If it can, the case usually fails. Once those gates are passed, siting's tied to the holding, the dwelling proportionate to the need, and the usual strands of design, amenity, highways and drainage assessed, with heritage, habitats or landscape duties where engaged.

Preference to live on site, retirement or succession planning, equity release — little weight. The decisive question is a proven essential functional need existing accommodation can't meet, and a financially sound enterprise. Conditions typically include an agricultural occupancy condition, a tie to the holding, removal of permitted-development rights, and often a temporary consent first — and the guide covers removing that occupancy condition later.

title: Applying it: a change of use
paras: A change of use. First, is permission even needed — the flexibility within the Use Classes Order, and prior-approval routes like Class M-A and Class Q, may mean it isn't. If it is, two questions: is the loss of the existing use acceptable, and is the new use acceptable here?

The loss — of employment land, a community facility, retail vitality — carries weight depending on demand evidence and marketing; an authority resisting the loss of employment land without that evidence is on weak ground. The new use turns on its amenity impacts — noise, hours, odour, traffic — and compatibility with neighbours, with highways, flood risk and contamination as relevant. For main town-centre uses in edge or out-of-centre locations, the sequential and impact tests apply. Heritage duties if listed or in a conservation area; habitats, rarely.

Competition or loss of trade to a rival isn't material, nor the operator's identity, nor licensing or environmental permitting absent a land-use overlap. The decisive question is whether the loss is justified and the new use compatible with its surroundings. Conditions commonly control hours, noise and odour, parking and servicing — and may restrict the Use Classes flexibility where justified.

title: Applying it: a replacement dwelling
paras: A replacement dwelling in the countryside turns first on a threshold — is there an existing lawful dwelling capable of being replaced? One whose residential use has been abandoned, or was never lawful, can't simply be replaced. So abandonment and lawfulness come first.

If there is a lawful dwelling, it's scale and siting. Many plans resist a disproportionate increase in size over the original, and landscape impact rises with bulk. The replacement should sit on or near the existing footprint — a materially different position is really a new dwelling in disguise. Landscape and character, amenity, highways and drainage follow. And ecology: protected species, particularly bats, are common in rural buildings and act as a hard constraint, needing survey and, where required, a licence. Heritage duties if it's designated.

A wish for a larger house, and the usual view and value points, aren't material. The decisive question is whether there's a lawful dwelling to replace, and whether the replacement is proportionate — no more harmful to the countryside than what it replaces. Conditions typically require demolition of the existing dwelling before, or within a set period of, occupation; removal of permitted-development rights; materials; and ecological mitigation — with a cross-reference in the guide on abandonment.

title: Applying it: a minor commercial scheme
paras: A minor commercial or employment scheme turns on whether the use is acceptable here, and whether it protects residential amenity and highway safety — amenity being the usual reason these get refused in or near residential areas.

On amenity: noise, hours, odour, light and dust, especially where sensitive receptors adjoin. On highways: access, parking, servicing and manoeuvring. Economic benefit — jobs and investment — carries positive weight in proportion to scale. Loss of any other use, design, flood risk and contamination as relevant; heritage duties if designated, habitats rarely; and for main town-centre uses, the sequential test.

Competition, the operator's identity, and licensing or environmental permitting absent a land-use overlap aren't material. The decisive question is whether the use can coexist with its neighbours and the highway network without unacceptable harm. Conditions commonly control hours, noise limits, delivery and servicing times, parking, and the use itself — with a travel plan for larger schemes.

title: Applying it: 150 homes on a greenfield edge
paras: And finally, 150 homes on a greenfield edge. A major housing scheme brings the whole apparatus into play, an explicit planning balance. The principle comes first — is housing acceptable here, allocated or not, within or beyond the settlement boundary, consistent with the spatial strategy? Then the pivotal question: is the tilted balance engaged?

Settle the plan position, test the housing land supply, and see whether the presumption's engaged. If it is, you shift from 'does this accord with the plan' to whether the harms significantly and demonstrably outweigh the benefits, against national policy as a whole — after checking whether a protective policy gives a clear reason for refusal. Benefits to weigh: market and affordable housing, geared to need and any shortfall, often substantial where supply's short; economic activity; infrastructure and contributions; biodiversity net gain; public-realm and highway improvements. Harms: landscape and visual impact, with great weight if a protected landscape's engaged; loss of best and most versatile agricultural land; heritage, including the setting of designated assets; highways — where the residual cumulative impact must be 'severe' to refuse on capacity, plus a separate safety test; ecology; flood risk and drainage; and coalescence and character.

The statutory duties sit outside all that as constraints — habitats, with appropriate assessment where there's a likely significant effect, and heritage, with its considerable importance and weight. Planning obligations must each meet the three tests: necessary; directly related to the development; and fairly and reasonably related in scale and kind. The community infrastructure levy applies where the authority charges. And a process overlay: environmental impact assessment screening for Schedule 2 development against the thresholds, likely committee determination and call-in risk, and the right handling of objection volume — the merits are material, the number isn't. The decisive question is whether the tilt is engaged and, if so, whether the harms significantly and demonstrably outweigh the substantial benefit of housing delivery.
